bill.title: Relating to consideration of the Senate amendment to the bill (H.R. 4) to rescind certain budget authority proposed to be rescinded in special messages transmitted to the Congress by the President on June 3, 2025, in accordance with section 1012(a) of the Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974.
bill.latestActionText: Motion to reconsider laid on the table Agreed to without objection.
bill.officialSummary: This resolution adopts H.R. 4, the Rescissions Act of 2025, as amended by the Senate. Specifically, upon the resolution's passage, the House is deemed to have agreed to the Senate amendment and passed H.R. 4.

classification.plainSummary:
This resolution adopts H.R. 4, the Rescissions Act of 2025, as amended by the Senate. Specifically, upon the resolution's passage, the House is deemed to have agreed to the Senate amendment and passed H.R. 4.

This is a simple resolution concerning the operation of Congress. It carries no sector tags and no donor overlap is computed for it, because attributing an economic interest to a commemorative or procedural measure would be misleading.

plain.whatItDoes: This is Congress running its own house. It sets a rule, a seat or a date for Congress itself. It does not change any law.
plain.whoItTouches: Nobody directly — this is Congress handling its own affairs.
plain.everydayEffect: Nothing changes for you. No rule and no payment changes.
plain.source: From the bill title, and from the subject labels that library staff put on it.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
